sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: Contoso Ltd. has 12 Azure subscriptions that are all direct children of a management group named mg-contoso-prod. The tenant also contains other subscriptions that are outside mg-contoso-prod. The security team must grant the Reader role to a Microsoft Entra group named SecOps-Auditors for all 12 subscriptions, and for those subscriptions only, by creating a single role assignment. At which scope should you create the role assignment?
opzione_c: The Tenant Root Group management group
spiegazione: Correct: a. Azure RBAC supports four scope levels - management group, subscription, resource group, and resource - structured in a parent-child relationship, and lower levels inherit role permissions from higher levels. A single Reader assignment on mg-contoso-prod inherits to every subscription under it, which is exactly the 12 target subscriptions and nothing else. Wrong: b. Assigning Reader on each subscription produces the required access but creates 12 role assignments, not the single assignment the requirement specifies. Wrong: c. The Tenant Root Group is a valid scope and would be one assignment, but everything in the directory folds up to the root management group, so the assignment would also grant Reader on the subscriptions outside mg-contoso-prod, violating the 'those subscriptions only' requirement. Wrong: d. The Microsoft Entra tenant is not an Azure RBAC scope. Microsoft Entra ID and Azure resources are secured independently; Microsoft Entra role assignments do not grant access to Azure resources.

domanda: While reviewing the Access control (IAM) page of a resource group, an administrator opens the Deny assignments tab and finds an entry that nobody on the team remembers creating. The administrator now wants to apply an equivalent deny assignment to a second resource group. Which statement correctly describes how deny assignments are created?
opzione_a: You can't directly create deny assignments; they're created and managed by Azure, although specifying deny settings when you create a deployment stack causes Azure to create one.
opzione_b: On the Access control (IAM) page, select Add and then select Add deny assignment, and choose the principal and the actions to deny.
opzione_c: Run the New-AzDenyAssignment cmdlet in Az PowerShell and specify the principal, the denied actions, and the scope.
opzione_d: Add the actions you want to block to the NotActions property of a custom role definition, then assign that custom role at the target scope.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft Learn states explicitly that 'You can't directly create your own deny assignments. Deny assignments are created and managed by Azure.' The documented way to cause one to exist is to specify deny settings when creating a deployment stack, which creates a deny assignment owned by the deployment stack resources. All deny assignments are currently system protected (IsSystemProtected is Yes in all cases). Wrong: b. There is no Add deny assignment action in Access control (IAM). The Deny assignments tab is read-only and only lists deny assignments at or inherited to the scope; viewing requires Microsoft.Authorization/denyAssignments/read. Wrong: c. Az PowerShell exposes Get-AzDenyAssignment for listing deny assignments, but there is no supported cmdlet to create one, because creation is reserved to Azure. Wrong: d. NotActions is not a deny rule. Microsoft Learn states 'NotActions is not a deny rule - it is simply a convenient way to create a set of allowed actions when specific actions need to be excluded.' If a second role assignment grants the same action, the user can still perform it, so NotActions cannot replicate a deny assignment.
tags: azure rbac,deny assignments,deployment stacks,system protected,access control iam

domanda: The following strings are Azure RBAC scopes taken from a role assignment audit. Arrange the five scopes in order from the broadest (least specific) scope to the most specific scope.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, d, a, e, c. Microsoft Learn states that scopes are structured in a parent-child relationship and that 'Each level of hierarchy makes the scope more specific,' with management groups having 'the broadest (least specific) scope.' Option b is a management group scope, which uses the /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{managementGroupName} format and sits above subscriptions. Option d is the subscription scope. Option a adds /resourceGroups/{name}, narrowing to a resource group inside that subscription. Option e adds /providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/{name}, narrowing to a single storage account resource in that resource group. Option c is the narrowest: it extends the storage account scope with /blobServices/default/containers/blob-container-01, targeting one blob container (a child resource). Any other ordering contradicts the documented hierarchy, because each additional identifier separated by the slash (/) character makes the scope more specific, and lower levels inherit role permissions from higher levels.

domanda: A custom role named VM Operations has its Actions property set to Microsoft.Compute/* and its NotActions property set to Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete. A user named Dana is assigned the VM Operations custom role at the scope of a resource group named rg-app01. Dana is also assigned the built-in Virtual Machine Contributor role at the rg-app01 scope. No deny assignments exist. Dana attempts to delete a virtual machine in rg-app01. What is the result, and why?
opzione_a: The deletion succeeds, because Azure RBAC is an additive model and NotActions is not a deny rule.
opzione_b: The deletion fails, because a NotActions entry in any assigned role removes that action from the user's effective permissions across all role assignments.
opzione_c: The deletion fails, because when two roles are assigned at the same scope, the more restrictive role definition takes precedence.
opzione_d: The deletion succeeds only if Dana is additionally assigned the Owner role at the subscription scope.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft Learn states 'Azure RBAC is an additive model, so your effective permissions are the sum of your role assignments,' and specifically notes that 'If a user is assigned a role that excludes an action in NotActions, and is assigned a second role that grants access to the same action, the user is allowed to perform that action. NotActions is not a deny rule.' The Virtual Machine Contributor assignment independently grants the delete action, so Dana can delete the VM. Wrong: b. NotActions is scoped to the single role definition it belongs to: effective permissions for that role are computed as Actions - NotActions. It does not subtract the action from other role assignments. Wrong: c. Azure RBAC has no 'most restrictive wins' precedence between role assignments. Only deny assignments block access that a role assignment grants, and Azure Resource Manager evaluates deny assignments before narrowing role assignments. Wrong: d. Owner at the subscription scope is unnecessary. The existing Virtual Machine Contributor assignment at rg-app01 already includes the delete action, and adding a broader assignment is not a prerequisite for the additive model to apply.
tags: azure rbac,notactions,custom role,additive model,effective permissions,virtual machine contributor

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: An engineer authors an Azure custom role that includes the DataActions entry Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/read and sets AssignableScopes to a single management group named mg-data. Azure creates the role definition successfully. However, when the engineer tries to assign the role at the mg-data management group scope, the assignment fails. What is the reason?
opzione_a: Custom roles that contain DataActions can't be assigned at management group scope, but the role can be assigned at the subscriptions, resource groups, or resources under mg-data.
opzione_b: AssignableScopes must include the root scope (/) before a custom role can be assigned at any management group scope.
opzione_c: A custom role can list only one management group in AssignableScopes, so mg-data must be replaced with the Tenant Root Group.
opzione_d: Data plane permissions can't be granted through Azure RBAC role definitions and must be assigned in the Microsoft Entra admin center instead.
spiegazione: Correct: a. The documented custom role limits state 'Custom roles with DataActions can't be assigned at the management group scope' and clarify: 'You can create a custom role with DataActions and one management group in AssignableScopes. You can't assign the custom role at the management group scope itself; however, you can assign the custom role at the scope of the subscriptions within the management group.' This is why the definition was created but the assignment failed. Wrong: b. Custom roles cannot set AssignableScopes to the root scope (/) at all - that is an explicit documented limit. The root scope is reserved for built-in roles. Wrong: c. The one-management-group rule is real, but the role already lists exactly one management group (mg-data), so it isn't violated. Swapping in the Tenant Root Group would not help, because the DataActions restriction applies to any management group scope. Wrong: d. Azure RBAC does support data plane permissions: the same authorization model used for control plane actions has been extended to data plane actions via the DataActions and NotDataActions properties. Built-in roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader use DataActions.

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: A platform team member named Priya must be able to assign and remove Azure role assignments for other users on a resource group named rg-shared. Priya must not be able to create or modify Azure Policy assignments, and she must not be able to manage the resources in rg-shared. You must follow the principle of least privilege and use a built-in role. Which role should you assign to Priya at the rg-shared scope?
spiegazione: Correct: d. The Role Based Access Control Administrator role is described as 'Manage access to Azure resources by assigning roles using Azure RBAC. This role does not allow you to manage access using other ways, such as Azure Policy.' Its Actions are exactly Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/delete, */read, and Microsoft.Support/*, which lets Priya add and remove role assignments and read resources, but not write to resources or to policy assignments. Wrong: a. Owner has Actions of * with no NotActions, granting full management of all resources plus role assignment - far more than required. Wrong: b. Contributor's NotActions include Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete, so Contributor explicitly cannot assign roles; it also grants full resource management, which is not wanted. Wrong: c. User Access Administrator's Actions are */read, Microsoft.Authorization/*, and Microsoft.Support/*. The Microsoft.Authorization/* wildcard includes Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/*, so it would let Priya create and modify Azure Policy assignments, breaking the stated requirement and least privilege.
tags: azure rbac,built-in roles,role based access control administrator,user access administrator,least privilege,delegation

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: You are authoring an Azure custom role definition for the Contoso tenant and you are reviewing the rules that govern the AssignableScopes property. Which three statements are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: AssignableScopes can't be set to the root scope ("/").
opzione_b: Wildcards (*) can't be used in AssignableScopes.
opzione_c: You can define only one management group in the AssignableScopes of a custom role.
opzione_d: AssignableScopes must contain at least one subscription, because management groups aren't supported as assignable scopes for custom roles.
opzione_e: Listing a scope in AssignableScopes grants the role's permissions at that scope, even when no role assignment exists.
spiegazione: Correct: a. The documented custom role limits state 'You cannot set AssignableScopes to the root scope ("/").' The root scope is reserved for built-in roles, whose AssignableScopes is "/". Correct: b. The limits also state 'You cannot use wildcards (*) in AssignableScopes. This wildcard restriction helps ensure a user can't potentially obtain access to a scope by updating the role definition.' Note that wildcards ARE allowed inside Actions, NotActions, DataActions, and NotDataActions strings (one wildcard per action string). Correct: c. 'You can define only one management group in AssignableScopes of a custom role.' This limits situations where role definitions and role assignments become disconnected when a subscription or management group moves to a different parent. Wrong: d. Management groups are explicitly supported: a valid example is "/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{groupId1}", and you can define a management group as an assignable scope so the role is available on that management group and everything under it. The requirement is only that you use at least one management group, subscription, or resource group. Wrong: e. AssignableScopes only specifies where the role is available for assignment (and controls who can create, update, delete, or view the custom role). It grants nothing by itself. Microsoft Learn states 'the level of access is determined by the custom role assignment (scope + role permissions + security principal) and not the AssignableScopes listed in the custom role.'
tags: azure rbac,custom role,assignablescopes,root scope,wildcards,management group,role definition

domanda: During an access review, an administrator examines a deny assignment that is listed on the Access control (IAM) page of an Azure subscription. Which three statements about deny assignments are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A deny assignment can exempt specific security principals from the block by using the ExcludePrincipals property.
opzione_b: A deny assignment blocks the specified actions even when a role assignment grants the principal access to those actions.
opzione_c: A deny assignment can be prevented from being inherited by child scopes by setting DoNotApplyToChildScopes to true.
opzione_d: A deny assignment does not apply to a principal that is assigned the Owner role at the same scope.
opzione_e: A deny assignment can block only data plane actions (DataActions) and never control plane actions.
spiegazione: Correct: a. ExcludePrincipals is a documented deny assignment property: 'An array of Microsoft Entra principal object IDs (user, group, service principal, or managed identity) to which the deny assignment does not apply.' Excluding principals is listed as a capability that deny assignments have and role assignments do not. Correct: b. Microsoft Learn defines a deny assignment as attaching 'a set of deny actions to a user, group, or service principal at a particular scope for the purpose of denying access. Deny assignments block users from performing specific Azure resource actions even if a role assignment grants them access.' In the evaluation logic, Azure Resource Manager checks deny assignments first: 'If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues.' Correct: c. DoNotApplyToChildScopes 'Specifies whether the deny assignment applies to child scopes. Default value is false,' and 'Prevent inheritance to child scopes' is listed as a deny assignment capability. Wrong: d. Owner is not exempt. Deny assignments are evaluated before role assignments and block access regardless of which role is assigned; the only documented exemption mechanism is ExcludePrincipals. Deny assignments even apply to classic subscription administrator assignments. Wrong: e. A deny assignment requires at least one Actions or one DataActions entry and supports Permissions.Actions and Permissions.NotActions for control plane actions as well as Permissions.DataActions and Permissions.NotDataActions for data plane actions. Deployment stack deny assignments, for example, deny the control plane action */delete.

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: The operations team at Northwind Traders needs a single Azure custom role that meets the following requirements: team members can perform every action in the Microsoft.Compute resource provider except deleting virtual machines; the role must be available for assignment in two subscriptions, sub-prod01 and sub-prod02, that trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant. You author the role definition in JSON. Select the correct option for each drop-down.
opzione_a: Property that must contain "Microsoft.Compute/*": [Actions | DataActions | NotActions | AssignableScopes]
opzione_b: Property that must contain "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete": [Actions | DataActions | NotActions | NotDataActions]
opzione_c: Property that must contain the two subscription IDs: [Scope | AssignableScopes | Condition | NotActions]
opzione_d: Maximum number of custom roles allowed per Microsoft Entra tenant: [500 | 2000 | 4000 | 5000]
spiegazione: Drop-down 1 - Actions: The Actions property 'specifies the control plane actions that the role allows to be performed.' Microsoft.Compute/* 'Grants access to all actions for all resource types in the Microsoft.Compute resource provider,' which matches the requirement. DataActions holds only data plane actions (where isDataAction is true), and compute management operations are control plane actions. NotActions and AssignableScopes do not grant anything. Drop-down 2 - NotActions: NotActions 'specifies the control plane actions that are subtracted or excluded from the allowed Actions that have a wildcard (*),' and effective permissions are computed as Actions - NotActions. Because Actions uses the Microsoft.Compute/* wildcard, subtracting the delete action with NotActions is exactly the documented pattern. Actions would grant the delete instead of excluding it; NotDataActions only subtracts from DataActions, and virtual machine delete is not a data action. Drop-down 3 - AssignableScopes: AssignableScopes is 'an array of strings that specifies the scopes that the custom role is available for assignment,' and "/subscriptions/{subscriptionId1}", "/subscriptions/{subscriptionId2}" is the documented example for making a role available in two subscriptions. Custom roles can be shared between subscriptions that trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Scope is a property of a role assignment, not of a role definition; Condition holds an ABAC condition statement; NotActions holds excluded actions. Drop-down 4 - 5000: Microsoft Learn states 'There is a limit of 5,000 custom roles per tenant' and 'Each tenant can have up to 5000 custom roles.' 2000 is the limit only for Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet; 4000 is the role assignments limit per subscription; 500 is the role assignments limit per management group.

domanda:
Adventure Works has a management group named mg-adventureworks that contains a subscription named sub-prod. The sub-prod subscription contains a resource group named rg-finance. A user named Sam is assigned the Contributor role at the mg-adventureworks scope and the Reader role at the rg-finance scope. There are no deny assignments and no role assignment conditions. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. Sam can create a storage account in rg-finance.
2. The Reader role assignment at rg-finance reduces Sam's effective permissions in rg-finance to read-only.
3. Sam can assign the Reader role to another user at the sub-prod scope.
opzione_a: Sam can create a storage account in rg-finance.
opzione_b: The Reader role assignment at rg-finance reduces Sam's effective permissions in rg-finance to read-only.
opzione_c: Sam can assign the Reader role to another user at the sub-prod scope.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: Scopes are structured in a parent-child relationship and 'Lower levels inherit role permissions from higher levels.' The Contributor assignment at mg-adventureworks therefore inherits to sub-prod and to rg-finance. Contributor's Actions are * (create and manage resources of all types), so Sam can create a storage account in rg-finance. Statement 2 - No: Azure RBAC is an additive model, so effective permissions are the sum of the role assignments, not the intersection. Microsoft Learn uses this exact example: a user granted Contributor at subscription scope and Reader on a resource group has 'effectively the Contributor role for the subscription. Therefore, in this case, the Reader role assignment has no impact.' A lower-scope Reader assignment cannot subtract permissions granted at a higher scope; only a deny assignment blocks access that a role assignment grants. Statement 3 - No: Contributor 'Grants full access to manage all resources, but does not allow you to assign roles in Azure RBAC.' Its NotActions include Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete, which subtract Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write from the * in Actions. Reader grants only read access and adds nothing here, so Sam has no effective permission to create a role assignment at sub-prod.

sotto_argomento: Create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles, including Azure roles and Microsoft Entra roles
domanda: A custom role named Sandbox Operator has its AssignableScopes set to /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/mg-sandbox. The role is assigned to a Microsoft Entra group at the scope of a subscription named sub-dev01, which is currently a child of mg-sandbox. A governance change requires sub-dev01 to be moved so that it becomes a child of a different management group named mg-corp. The move fails with an error stating that it would break the relationship between the role assignment and the role definition. Which action resolves the issue while keeping the existing role assignment on sub-dev01 in place?
opzione_a: Add /subscriptions/{sub-dev01-id} to the AssignableScopes of the Sandbox Operator role, then move the subscription.
opzione_b: Add /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/mg-corp as a second management group in the AssignableScopes of the Sandbox Operator role, then move the subscription.
opzione_c: Remove the Sandbox Operator role assignment from sub-dev01, then move the subscription.
opzione_d: Set the AssignableScopes of the Sandbox Operator role to the root scope ("/"), then move the subscription.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Moving sub-dev01 out from under mg-sandbox breaks the hierarchy path from the role assignment on the subscription up to the role definition on the management group, which is why Azure blocks the move. Microsoft Learn lists 'Add the subscription to the role definition's assignable scope' as a documented fix. AssignableScopes accepts subscriptions alongside a management group, so after adding the sub-dev01 scope the definition remains reachable from the assignment regardless of the new parent, and the assignment survives. Wrong: b. 'You can define only one management group in the assignable scopes of a new role.' The definition already contains mg-sandbox, so mg-corp cannot be added as a second management group. Wrong: c. Removing the role assignment before the move is a documented option and would allow the move to succeed, but it does not satisfy the requirement to keep the existing role assignment on sub-dev01 in place - the access would have to be recreated afterwards. Wrong: d. Custom roles cannot use the root scope: 'You cannot set AssignableScopes to the root scope ("/").' The root scope is reserved for built-in roles. (Retargeting AssignableScopes to the root management group would be valid, but that is a management group, not the root scope "/".)
tags: azure rbac,custom role,assignablescopes,management group,move subscription,troubleshooting,role definition

sotto_argomento: Provide access to Azure resources by assigning roles at different scopes
domanda: An onboarding pipeline that grants developers access to resources in a large Azure subscription starts failing with the error: No more role assignments can be created (code: RoleAssignmentLimitExceeded). Investigation shows that the subscription has accumulated thousands of individual role assignments, many of them granting the same built-in role to different users at the same resource group scope. Which action resolves the problem?
opzione_a: Open an Azure support request to increase the role assignment limit for the subscription.
opzione_b: Add the developers to Microsoft Entra groups and replace the individual role assignments with a single role assignment for each group at the same scope.
opzione_c: Create the remaining role assignments at resource scope instead of resource group scope, because only role assignments at subscription and resource group scopes count toward the limit.
opzione_d: Convert the redundant role assignments into deny assignments, which are not counted against the role assignment limit.
spiegazione: Correct: b. Azure supports up to 4000 role assignments per subscription, and the documented Solution 1 is to 'Replace principal-based role assignments with group-based role assignments': add principals to groups and assign roles to the groups instead. This works because role assignments are transitive for groups, so every member inherits the permissions from the single group assignment, collapsing many assignments into one. Wrong: a. Microsoft Learn states explicitly: 'The 4000 role assignments limit per subscription is fixed and cannot be increased.' A support request cannot raise it. Wrong: c. The limit 'includes role assignments at the subscription, resource group, and resource scopes,' so moving assignments to resource scope does not help. (Only management group scope assignments are excluded from the per-subscription limit, and those are governed by a separate limit of 500 per management group.) Wrong: d. You can't directly create deny assignments - they're created and managed by Azure - and deny assignments block access rather than grant it, so they cannot replace role assignments that are meant to give developers access.

domanda: Fabrikam organizes its Azure estate as follows. A management group named mg-prod contains a subscription named sub-01. The sub-01 subscription contains two resource groups, rg-web and rg-data. A Microsoft Entra group named G1 is assigned the Reader role at the mg-prod scope and the Contributor role at the rg-web scope. A deployment stack manages the resources in rg-web and was created with a deny settings mode of DenyDelete, applying to All Principals with no excluded principals and no excluded actions. User1 is a member of G1. Select the correct option for each drop-down.
opzione_a: User1's effective access to a storage account in rg-data: [No access | Read only | Read and write | Full control including delete]
opzione_b: User1 can create a new virtual machine in rg-web: [Yes | No]
opzione_c: User1 can delete a resource that is managed by the deployment stack in rg-web: [Yes | No]
opzione_d: If User1 is also assigned the Owner role at the sub-01 scope, User1 can delete a resource that is managed by the deployment stack in rg-web: [Yes | No]
spiegazione: Drop-down 1 - Read only: Lower levels inherit role permissions from higher levels, so the Reader assignment at mg-prod inherits to sub-01 and to rg-data. Role assignments are transitive for groups, so User1 receives G1's permissions. The Contributor assignment applies only at the rg-web scope and does not reach rg-data, and the deny assignment is scoped to rg-web. User1 therefore has Reader only in rg-data. (Note that Reader is a control plane role: User1 could see the storage account but not read the blob data, because control plane access is not inherited to the data plane.) Drop-down 2 - Yes: Azure RBAC is additive, so at rg-web User1's effective permissions are the sum of Reader (inherited from mg-prod) and Contributor (assigned at rg-web), which is effectively Contributor. Contributor's Actions are *, so User1 can create a virtual machine. The deny settings mode is DenyDelete, which prohibits delete operations only - it does not block write operations. Drop-down 3 - No: Specifying deny settings when creating a deployment stack causes Azure to create a deny assignment owned by the deployment stack. A deny assignment 'blocks users from performing specific Azure resource actions even if a role assignment grants them access,' and Azure Resource Manager evaluates deny assignments before role assignments: 'If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues.' The deny assignment targets All Principals with no excluded principals, so User1 is blocked from deleting managed resources despite holding Contributor. Drop-down 4 - No: Adding the Owner role changes nothing, because deny assignments take precedence over role assignments regardless of how privileged the role is. The only documented way to exempt an identity is the ExcludePrincipals property of the deny assignment, which the deployment stack populates from its excluded principals setting - and the scenario states there are none.
tags: azure rbac,deny assignments,deployment stacks,denydelete,inheritance,additive model,evaluation logic,effective permissions
